stories.summary: DaVinci Resolve is now one of the big three editing programs, and anyone can download it free and get state-of-the-art editing and colour grading. Amit points out that in 2010, when it only did colour grading, it cost $800,000. India had no copy at all, so Bollywood films were sent to Hollywood for colour grading and shipped back, with the rental added to the film's costs.
stories.insight: In about a decade, tools that only a few studios could afford became consumer-grade and nearly free. The means of production now sit with individual creators, which is what lets two people run their own show.
stories.quote: There wasn't one in India because it cost eight hundred thousand dollars for color grading.

stories.topic: How Europe learned to be a state
stories.summary: Ajay asks whether the large Swedish state appeared fully formed, and answers that it did not. Through the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries, European states did essentially two things. They ran a fiscal system to raise taxes (the 'fiscus'), and they waged war, along with the contracting and technology that arms required. Over centuries of doing these narrow jobs they learned HR, contracting, checks and balances, how to control corruption, how to solve principal-agent problems, and how to keep the military in its barracks within a liberal democracy. Only after that was the capability applied to new problems such as vaccines.
stories.insight: State capacity is learned slowly, through narrow and repeated practice over generations. Taking on a wide scope before the capability exists invites failure. This is why Ajay wants India to spend 25 to 50 years mastering the basics.
stories.quote: It took hundreds of years, but around that, they learned how to be a state.

stories.summary: Ajay is explaining why secrecy makes a state function harder to run well. He notes that the military is admired and respected but shrouded in secrecy. Once the shooting started in Putin's war, the world discovered mind-blowing failures inside the Russian military. These had been hidden behind pompous parades, nationalism and militarism.
stories.insight: Secrecy removes the scrutiny that exposes malfeasance, so the most opaque parts of the state tend to hide the most failure. A grand spectacle tells you nothing about whether the institution actually works.
stories.quote: While there is a lot of admiration and respect for the military, it is also the case that the military is shrouded in secrecy. And that's likely to be the cover for a lot of state failure.

stories.topic: Kerala's diabetes, Bihar's hunger, Delhi's schemes
stories.summary: Amit draws on two Seen and the Unseen episodes: one with Pranay Kotasthane on centrally sponsored schemes, and one with RS Nilakantan on his book about South India. Kerala's health problem is diabetes and obesity, while Bihar and other parts of north and central India face malnourishment. Ideally each state would get a health budget and decide locally how to tackle its own problem. Instead, central schemes are designed in Delhi around nearby northern priorities and miss local needs.
stories.insight: A single scheme designed for a country this diverse solves the designer's local problem, not the citizen's. This is a concrete case for the subsidiarity principle.
stories.quote: the needs of the North and the South are so different. But the priorities of the North dictate public policy.

recommendations.item: Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation at the end of the episode, after the toolkit for thinking about state intervention.
recommendations.reason: The book examines how hard it is for states and bureaucracies to 'see' society, and how often the state inflicts cruelty and violence on people when it does see them. Ajay calls it a great cautionary book on the fraught relationship between the individual and the state. He and Kelkar borrowed its idea of 'state legibility' to coin 'premature state legibility' for the debates over India's digital systems.

recommendations.item: Cicada
recommendations.creator: Shaun Tan
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation. It was first recommended to him on a Seen and the Unseen episode about motherhood, and the copy he holds up is borrowed from editor Nomsita.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Shaun Tan a great illustrator, writer and artist and the book 'marvelous'. He deliberately says nothing about its contents, only asks you to read it.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit plugs it right after Ajay lays out the four buckets of market failure, and again before the book recommendations.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a masterpiece. It is the source of the toolkit used in this episode: market failure, the extended complexity test for state intervention, and the principle of choosing the least intrusive intervention.

recommendations.item: The Art and Science of Economic Policy (Episode 154 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned alongside In Service of the Republic. Amit says he has recorded with 'both eminences'.
recommendations.reason: A long conversation with both authors of the book behind this episode's framework.

recommendations.item: State Building
recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Amit's recap of the previous episode, which used Fukuyama's scale of state strength and scope.
recommendations.reason: It gives the strength-versus-scope lens. The ideal is a strong state with limited scope. India is a weak state that does too much, which Amit calls the worst of both worlds.

recommendations.item: Understanding the State (Episode 25 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The first part of the multi-episode series on the state. Amit summarises it at the start.
recommendations.reason: It sets up the foundations this episode builds on: the state is always coercive, every intervention has to be justified, and the strength-versus-scope framework.

recommendations.item: Solutions When the Solution is the Problem: Arraying the Disarray in Development
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock
recommendations.context: Ajay cites this 2004 paper while building the 'chai conversation' test for how hard a state intervention will be.
recommendations.reason: It supplies the first two dimensions of the test. Interventions involving many transactions, or a lot of discretion for frontline staff, are harder to deliver. Kelkar and Shah later added stakes and secrecy.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah on the Dangers of Digital Public Infrastructure (Episode 72 of Brave New World)
recommendations.creator: Vasant Dhar
recommendations.context: Mentioned while Ajay defines public goods. The conversation was based on two chapters of the Kelkar-Shah book.
recommendations.reason: Ajay lays out his fundamental objection to India's so-called 'digital public goods'. By the strict definition they are generally rival and excludable, so they are not public goods at all.

recommendations.item: Public Choice: A Primer
recommendations.creator: Eomonn Butler
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes after Amit raises public choice theory and the neglected idea of 'state failure'.
recommendations.reason: People keep citing market failure to justify intervention, yet no one talks about state failure. Public choice theory explains why state failure is practically everywhere, and Amit wants to do a full episode on it.

recommendations.item: Amit Varma on Public Choice Theory (mashup of The Seen and the Unseen and The Pragati Podcast)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Show-notes companion to Amit's point that state failure deserves as much attention as market failure.
recommendations.reason: An audio introduction to the field Amit says explains why state failure is ubiquitous.

recommendations.item: Centrally Sponsored Government Schemes (Episode 20 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane
recommendations.context: Cited when Amit argues that government should be as local as possible.
recommendations.reason: This is where Amit learned how schemes designed in Delhi fail to fit the very different needs of different states.

recommendations.item: South India Would Like to Have a Word (Episode 320 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with RS Nilakantan
recommendations.context: Cited with the Kotasthane episode in the Kerala-versus-Bihar example.
recommendations.reason: It explores how differently South India's needs look from the North's, even though the North's priorities drive national policy.

recommendations.item: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit plugs it while discussing Kerala's problem with diabetes and obesity.
recommendations.reason: Amit's message, 'We can conquer diabetes. Yes, we can.'

recommendations.item: Yes Minister / Yes Prime Minister
recommendations.creator: Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay
recommendations.context: Amit quotes the series while arguing that the state doesn't need to act on every problem.
recommendations.reason: It supplies the perfect parody of policy reflexes, 'We must do something, this is something, therefore we must do this.'

recommendations.item: Johan Norberg's writings on Sweden's free-market rise
recommendations.creator: Johan Norberg
recommendations.context: Amit's reply to people who cite Scandinavian welfare states against the case for freedom.
recommendations.reason: Amit says Norberg shows in detail that the Nordic countries were model free-market economies that got rich before they became welfare states.

recommendations.item: Indian Colours
recommendations.context: Ajay explains where his art shirt comes from at the start of the episode.
recommendations.reason: It works with Indian artists and pays them royalties, as authors earn on books. Art printed on shirts, cups and stoles lets ordinary people surround themselves with beauty without spending lakhs on originals. Ajay says great art lights up your life.

recommendations.item: DaVinci Resolve
recommendations.context: Amit's example of how the means of production have become cheap.
recommendations.reason: The free version alone gives you state-of-the-art editing and the best colour grading, from software that once cost $800,000.

recommendations.item: $800,000 to Zero - The FASCINATING History of DaVinci Resolve
recommendations.creator: Learn Color Grading
recommendations.context: The video where Amit learned the DaVinci Resolve story, linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great video on how a once-unaffordable professional tool became free.

recommendations.item: RODE Wireless PRO
recommendations.creator: RODE
recommendations.context: The new mics that replaced the hosts' boom arms in this episode.
recommendations.reason: They record in 32-bit float, so there is no fight over levels while recording and no clipping. Everything can be fixed afterwards, much like shooting RAW in photography.

recommendations.item: How 32-bit Float Recording Works on the Wireless PRO
recommendations.context: Show-notes link for the 32-bit float discussion that opens the episode.
recommendations.reason: For anyone curious about the technology Ajay admits he 'only dimly' understands.

recommendations.item: The RODE Wireless PRO is NUTS!
recommendations.creator: DLSR Video Shooter
recommendations.context: Show-notes link reviewing the mics introduced in this episode.
recommendations.reason: A hands-on review of the gear behind the hosts' new 'level of human freedom'.

recommendations.item: Pune Public Policy Festival (January 19-20, 2024)
recommendations.context: The episode's sponsor.
recommendations.reason: Young professionals meet bureaucrats, economists and thinkers around the theme of trade-offs: environment versus growth, growth versus equality, technology versus privacy. Amit also likes that it pulls policy discussion back to Pune, once called the Oxford of the East, and away from Delhi.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Show-notes link, since this episode's framework treats freedom as the default.
recommendations.reason: It makes the case for freedom that this whole toolkit rests on.

core_ideas.concept: Every state action is justified violence
core_ideas.explanation: The state is always coercive, and it pays for everything through taxes it collects by force. We accept this because we need it to protect our rights. So every time someone says 'the state should do X', they are proposing violence and owe a justification. The state is not a benevolent beast whose actions are free.
core_ideas.quote: every time we recommend that the state should do X or the state should do Y, we should be able to justify it. Because each time we are justifying violence.

core_ideas.explanation: This follows Fukuyama's two axes. Scope is how much the state meddles in. Strength is how well it does those things. The ideal is a strong state with limited scope. 'Strong' means robust democratic systems that resist radical swings and can enforce the rule of law. It does not mean a strongman.
core_ideas.quote: India happens to have a weak state that does too much. So it is the worst of both worlds.

core_ideas.concept: Market failure is a free lunch, not Robin Hood
core_ideas.explanation: Freedom is the baseline, and people should be left alone by default. Economists have identified a narrow class of problems where the right intervention can make some people better off without hurting anyone. That makes it something everyone can agree on, unlike populist redistribution or class warfare. Even a monopoly should be regulated in ways the monopolist could accept, not out of envy of the rich. A natural monopoly may only need its prices regulated, not to be broken up.
core_ideas.quote: Market failure is a class of problems where there is an analytical and a technical possibility that the correct kind of state intervention is a free lunch because it will make some people in society better off without harming anybody at all.

core_ideas.concept: The four buckets of market failure
core_ideas.explanation: 1. Market power: monopolies and oligopolies. 2. Externalities, meaning uncontracted spillovers. Positive ones include your education or vaccination benefiting me, which leads people to underinvest in them. Negative ones include smoking, loudspeakers and crime. 3. Asymmetric information: grandmothers and dentists cannot test medicine purity, check a restaurant's kitchen, or judge whether their bank is sound. 4. Public goods. Outside these four, freedom stays the default.
core_ideas.quote: So I've described four categories: public goods, asymmetric information, externalities, and market power. These are green lighted by the economists as market failure.

core_ideas.concept: A public good is not 'something good for the public'
core_ideas.explanation: Technically, a public good is non-rival and non-excludable. Non-rival means my use doesn't reduce yours: one woman walking safely doesn't use up the street's safety. Non-excludable means you couldn't even in theory exclude a newborn, as with clean air. North India's air pollution is therefore a true public-goods problem. Ajay would back taxing people to fly 10,000 drones over the Hindi heartland, spot every fire, and ticket whoever lit it. India's 'digital public goods', by contrast, are mostly rival and excludable.
core_ideas.quote: Again, the welfareist socialist impulse in India is anything that is good for the people is a public good, and that's just wrong. A public good is something that is non-rival and non-excludable.

core_ideas.concept: Economics hides technical terms in plain English
core_ideas.explanation: Unlike science, economics reuses ordinary words such as market failure, public good, adverse selection and moral hazard. They sound accessible but have precise meanings. A shop having only blue cushions when you wanted green is not a market failure. Amit adds that words like rights versus entitlements, or liberal and progressive, have drifted far from their original meanings.
core_ideas.quote: This is a bane of economics that in the field of economics we repurpose plain English words.

core_ideas.concept: Utilitarian claims assume knowledge is easy, so demand a high bar of proof
core_ideas.explanation: 'Freedom doesn't work here' is a claim about consequences. Amit warns that such claims often rest on engineering-style assumptions that 'if we do this, that will happen', and that rarely comes true. Consequences matter, but anyone who wants to override freedom should face a very high burden of proof. Otherwise market failure becomes a convenient excuse to crush freedom. Amit also notes that nobody talks about state failure, which public choice theory shows is everywhere.
core_ideas.quote: one of my issues with all utilitarian thinking is that it assumes that knowledge is easy. Knowledge is not easy. Knowledge is very difficult to come by.

core_ideas.concept: Freedom wins even if you don't value freedom
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay offers a second, value-neutral argument. Suppose you are a conservative who prizes order or tradition over liberty. Even so, defaulting to freedom and limiting the state to market failures it can actually fix is the objective path to prosperity. You don't need to share the moral premise to accept the economic one.
core_ideas.quote: As a card carrying economist, I'm saying to you that societies flourish when freedom is a baseline and government intervention is limited to the class of market failures where there can be a successful implementation.

core_ideas.concept: Business-friendly is the opposite of market-friendly
core_ideas.explanation: Market-friendly means competition and free entry, which benefits consumers. Business-friendly means protecting incumbents, who lobby for tariffs and regulations to keep rivals out. Amit argues that genuine monopolies are very rare in competitive markets. Most real monopolies trace back to cronyism or a state-created barrier to entry, or turn out to be defined wrongly.
core_ideas.quote: Market friendly means you have competition, anyone can enter. Business friendly means the existing businesses who are there. They want to keep competitors out, which hurts consumers.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's four-word diagnostic question for any problem in society: trace it to the act of coercion. In his experience, that is where the root of the problem always turns out to be.
core_ideas.quote: Where is the coercion? And where you identify the coercion, often, most of the time, in fact in my case always, you will find that the root of the problem is there.

core_ideas.concept: Market failure doesn't license intervention: implementation failure
core_ideas.explanation: Spotting a market failure only opens the question. Ajay's rule is not to rush in where angels fear to tread. Ask whether the state can actually succeed, and cheaply. Otherwise you create a corrupt bureaucracy that kicks private people around. Be willing to walk away, or to back out when an intervention isn't working.
core_ideas.quote: So living with a market failure is often better than living with a bad state intervention that claims to address that market failure and oftentimes fails to address it.

core_ideas.concept: The four-question 'chai conversation' test of difficulty
core_ideas.explanation: Pritchett and Woolcock (2004) supplied two questions, and Kelkar and Shah added two more. (1) Are there many transactions? (2) Do frontline staff have discretion? (3) Are the stakes high? (4) Is there secrecy? A polio drive has many transactions but no discretion, since staff just follow a manual, so it is easy to roll out. A truant teacher steals about ₹15,000 a month, so the effort put into misbehaviour is limited. In criminal justice the accused faces jail, so the pressure toward corruption goes to infinity. Secrecy, as in the military, hides failure. Four yes/no answers tell you whether you face an easy problem or a hard one.
core_ideas.quote: In these four zero one numbers, you've got a grip of the essence that some things are easy, some things are hard

core_ideas.concept: Pick the least intrusive intervention, and go to the root cause
core_ideas.explanation: Most market failures can be addressed in several ways, and each brings different winners and losers. Choose the one that intrudes least on people's lives, in line with the liberal dream of living on your own terms without thinking about the state. An intervention that touches your body is worse than one that doesn't. Knocking on your door is worse than not knocking, and entering your house is worse than standing at the door. The cheapest fix is usually at the root cause: clean the air rather than build hospitals, and build good roads rather than trauma centres at every highway exit.
core_ideas.quote: A good intervention is one that is the least intrusive in the lives of people.

core_ideas.explanation: Each government function belongs at the lowest level of government that can handle it. Local governments understand local problems, as with Kerala's diabetes versus Bihar's malnourishment. A scheme designed centrally imposes one region's priorities on everyone.
core_ideas.quote: The principle is called the subsidiarity principle. And this is one of the great ideas in economics, which asserts that every problem in government should be placed at the lowest level of government where it can be placed.

core_ideas.concept: You don't always have to do something
core_ideas.explanation: State capacity, money and bandwidth are limited, so every intervention has an opportunity cost. Before acting, ask whether this is the right thing to do and whether the state needs to do it at all. India hasn't yet solved basics like the rule of law, so spreading the state thinner carries a real cost.
core_ideas.quote: listen, government has limited capacity, limited money, limited bandwidth. You need to think about what are the core priorities

core_ideas.concept: Learning by doing: start with narrow scope
core_ideas.explanation: Every advanced economy took hundreds of years to learn to run a state. Ajay's advice for India is to master a few things first, such as police and judiciary, for 25 to 50 years. Only then should society debate widening the state's scope. Arguing over more or less welfare is premature while those basic problems remain unsolved.
core_ideas.quote: So it's always wise to start with a very low scope, start with a few narrow problems, and maybe for one or two generations, just learn how to do those few things.

core_ideas.concept: Rich first, welfare later; Swedish results need Swedish foundations
core_ideas.explanation: Amit makes two points about the Nordic countries. Behind their welfare states they keep great individual liberty, and starting a business there is far easier than in India. They also became rich as free-market economies before building welfare states, once state capacity existed. Ajay adds that you cannot copy one Swedish outcome without the surrounding environment that supports it.
core_ideas.quote: Swedish levels of the cashless economy is backed by Swedish levels of rule of law.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Opening on Ajay's big smile after the clunky boom arms were removed: 'I have the feeling one day I will disappear and you will be even happier.' (Amit)

The German philosopher mix-up. Amit is told he missed a chance to plug a German philosopher and asks what Immanuel Kant's categorical imperative has to do with it. Ajay means the proletariat owning the means of production: 'So you and I, humble slaves and producers, are no longer the subjects of the giant media companies.' The exchange lands on the pun that names the chapter: 'Who says Immanuel can't? Now Immanuel can.'

The boom-arm running gag. Ajay says the new mics give 'a new level of human freedom. We can wave our arms around.' He then builds it into the economics: by default people should 'swing their arms wildly and not be constrained by a boom arm required by a government regulator.' On externalities: 'my freedom to move my fist should be limited not just by the absence of the boom arm, but by the proximity of your nose.'

Ajay keeps casting Amit as 'the great dictator Amit Bhai' running the country over chai. Amit fires back: 'Mr. Shah is a great dictator. Mr. Shah with his authoritarian command over facts. Mr. Shah with his oppression of bad ideas. You are the problem here, let me tell you that.'

Ajay on food safety: 'Gentle reader, please Google gutter oil. It will blow your mind.' Amit, judging only from Ajay's face: 'I suspect it will blow your guts as well. ... don't tell me, don't tell me, continue.'

Amit teases Ajay's habit of calling things 'one of the great ideas in economics': 'how many are there? One of the greatest means kitne?' He closes the episode on the same note, calling Ajay 'one of the greatest hosts of Everything is Everything', a show that has two hosts.
Yes Minister / Yes Prime Minister (Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay), quoted for the policymaker's fallacy: 'we must do something, this is something, therefore we must do this.'

Marx, unnamed: Ajay sets the market-failure worldview against 'the great German philosopher who claimed that the history of mankind is a history of class warfare'. He also invokes Robin Hood: 'We're not doing Robin Hood.'
Amit's analogy for 32-bit float audio: it is like RAW for photographs. It captures all the information, so levels can be adjusted afterwards and clipping disappears.
Pune as 'the Oxford of the East', an intellectual hub whose centre of gravity shifted to Delhi after independence. Amit uses it to explain why the Pune Public Policy Festival matters.
